title: Collect and summarize production prompt-length distribution (anonymized) for mixed-workload scheduler thresholds
creator: Talia Benson
project: Mixed-workload scheduler prototype (Serving Runtime Performance: Kernel + Scheduling)
description:
Goal
- Pull anonymized prompt/context length distribution stats from production traffic (Hosted + Dedicated), propose “short/long” threshold candidates for scheduler classification, and publish a brief summary to Drive/Confluence for design + benchmarking alignment.

Context
- We’re seeing head-of-line blocking under mixed prompt-length distributions (short chat prompts interleaved with long-context prompts). Scheduler policy needs a stable, defensible threshold (or a small set of thresholds by SKU/model) to split traffic into classes.

Scope
- Aggregate-only stats (no raw prompts).
- Segment by: endpoint type (chat vs generate), deployment mode (Hosted vs Dedicated), and model family bucket ("7–13B", "30–40B", "70B+"), plus time-of-day sanity check.
- Produce candidates for short/long cutoff + quick sensitivity analysis.

Non-goals
- Not a full multi-tenant QoS tier definition.
- Not a product-facing report; internal runtime design input only.

Method
1) Source data
- Pulled from serving request logs and tracing spans via telemetry pipeline (request metadata only): prompt_tokens, max_new_tokens, total_context_tokens (when available), prefill_time_ms, time_in_queue_ms.
- Sample window: 7 days ending 2025-12-08, excluding known incident windows flagged by SRE.

2) Anonymization & safeguards
- Aggregated metrics only; no prompt text; no user identifiers in exports.
- Bucketing: token counts bucketed to reduce re-identification risk (e.g., 0–64, 65–128, …, 4097–8192, 8193+).
- Dedicated pool IDs mapped to coarse “SKU class” (A100-80GB / H100-80GB / L40S) before leaving the secure analytics workspace.

3) Outputs computed
- Request-weighted distribution (percent of requests by prompt/context length bucket).
- Token-weighted distribution (percent of total prompt tokens by bucket).
- Relationship to latency: median/p95 TTFT and prefill_time_ms by bucket (rough correlation, not causal).

Findings (high level)
A) Request-weighted prompt_tokens distribution (Hosted + Dedicated combined)
- <=128 tokens: ~46% of requests
- <=256 tokens: ~68% of requests
- <=512 tokens: ~81% of requests
- <=1024 tokens: ~90% of requests
- >2048 tokens: ~6–9% of requests (varies by model family)

B) Token-weighted distribution (why long prompts dominate GPU time)
- Requests >2048 tokens represent single-digit % of requests but ~45–60% of total prompt tokens (prefill work).
- Long-context traffic is disproportionately present in:
  - Dedicated workloads running retrieval-heavy pipelines
  - Batch jobs misrouted through interactive endpoints during peak hours (see notes below)

C) Latency correlation (indicative)
- TTFT p95 and prefill_time_ms increase superlinearly after ~512–768 prompt tokens depending on model family.
- Under mixed workloads, queueing amplification shows up when long-prefill requests are admitted into the same batch selection path as short interactive prompts.

Threshold candidates (for scheduler “short vs long” classification)
Candidate 1: Static threshold at 512 prompt tokens
- Pros: Covers ~80% of requests as “short”; simple mental model; lines up with visible TTFT inflection.
- Cons: Some long-context “medium” prompts (513–900) still have latency sensitivity; could push too much traffic into “long” for smaller models.

Candidate 2: Static threshold at 384 prompt tokens (more aggressive protection for short)
- Pros: Improves protection for interactive chat; increases separation for mixed 80/20 scenarios.
- Cons: Moves ~10–15% more traffic into “long” class; may reduce throughput if long queue becomes consistently non-empty without tuned aging/token budgets.

Candidate 3: Two-dimensional rule (preferred for prototype if plumbing allows)
- “Short” if prompt_tokens <= 512 AND predicted_prefill_cost_ms <= X
- Predicted_prefill_cost_ms derived from prompt_tokens * model_factor * kv_cache_state (coarse).
- Pros: More stable across models/SKUs; reduces misclassification of short tokens with unexpectedly heavy prefill.
- Cons: Requires keeping prediction stable enough to avoid thrash; more knobs to tune.

Recommendation (for design + benchmarks)
- Use 512 prompt_tokens as the default “short/long” split for first canary, with a config knob to move between 384/512.
- For benchmarks, include sweeps at 384 and 512 to quantify p95 gains vs throughput/fairness.
- If we see instability across SKUs/models, revisit Candidate 3 (cost-based) but keep it behind a separate flag to avoid compounding variables.

Notes / anomalies observed
- A small number of traffic sources are sending max_new_tokens very high together with long prompts; these requests correlate with queue growth during peak hours. Flagged to runtime + SRE to confirm whether backpressure/admission control is working as expected.
- Some Dedicated pools show bimodal distributions (tiny prompts + very large prompts). This aligns with customer reports and supports the two-queue approach.

Artifacts
- Drive: mixed-workload-trace-analysis-sheet (token bucket tables + sensitivity)
  - sources/google_drive/shared_drives/engineering/serving-runtime/mixed-workload-trace-analysis-sheet.json
- Confluence: linked summary added to scheduler design (section “Production distributions & threshold rationale”)
  - sources/confluence/eng-serving-runtime/kernel-and-scheduling/mixed-workload-scheduler-prototype-design.json

Impact on next steps
- Informed default threshold knob for ENG-2432 (classification) and benchmark mixes for ENG-2449.
- Provided target distributions for “80/20 short/long” synthetic workloads (where “short” is <=512 prompt tokens).

Open questions
- Do we want separate thresholds per model family in the prototype, or keep one global default for canary to reduce config surface?
- Should we classify by total_context_tokens (prompt + cache reuse) when available, rather than prompt_tokens alone, to better capture long-context chat sessions?

Acceptance criteria
- Summary doc published and linked from design ticket.
- Threshold candidates documented with pros/cons.
- Raw export does not contain prompt content or identifiers; only aggregate buckets.

Done definition
- Completed analysis, published Drive sheet + Confluence summary, and posted highlights to #eng-runtime.
